clues: It is the only one of Barcroft's four hypoxia categories characterized by a low arterial PaO2
Common causes include high altitude, hypoventilation, V/Q mismatch, and right-to-left shunts
It occurs when inadequate pulmonary gas exchange fails to oxygenate arterial blood normally
Cyanide poisoning is the classic lethal cause of this condition
Venous blood returns bright red with an abnormally narrowed arteriovenous oxygen difference
Arterial PO2 and blood flow are normal, but poisoned mitochondrial cytochrome oxidase cannot use oxygen
It widens the arteriovenous oxygen content difference because slow blood transit maximizes tissue extraction
Cardiogenic shock, severe heart failure, and acute arterial embolism are typical causes
Also called ischemic hypoxia, it occurs when tissue perfusion is inadequate despite normal arterial PaO2

terms.sub: Oxygen Toxicity (Paul Bert and Lorrain Smith Effects)
clues: It occurs during acute exposure to hyperbaric oxygen above 2 atmospheres absolute
SCUBA divers breathing nitrox too deep risk this complication underwater
It represents central nervous system oxygen toxicity manifesting with visual auras, twitching, and seizures

terms.sub: Oxygen Toxicity (Paul Bert and Lorrain Smith Effects)
clues: It develops after prolonged normobaric ventilation with FiO2 greater than 0.60 for over 24 to 48 hours
Reactive oxygen species injure alveolar epithelium and inactivate pulmonary surfactant
It represents pulmonary oxygen toxicity causing tracheobronchitis, atelectasis, and ARDS-like edema
Breathing 100% oxygen washes out poorly soluble nitrogen that normally stents alveoli open
Behind mucus-plugged or poorly ventilated airways, rapid O2 uptake into capillaries collapses the alveolus
It is a common complication of prolonged high-FiO2 mechanical ventilation

terms.sub: High-Altitude Illnesses (AMS, HAPE, HACE, Chronic Mountain Sickness)
clues: Exaggerated, uneven hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction causes capillary stress failure and protein-rich alveolar fluid
Patients develop severe exertional then resting dyspnea, crackles, and pink frothy sputum above 2,500 meters
Immediate descent, supplemental oxygen, and nifedipine are the mainstays of treatment

terms.sub: High-Altitude Illnesses (AMS, HAPE, HACE, Chronic Mountain Sickness)
clues: Truncal ataxia and altered mental status mark its progression from acute mountain sickness
Hypoxic cerebral vasodilation and blood-brain barrier disruption produce vasogenic brain swelling
It is treated emergently with descent, oxygen, and dexamethasone

terms.sub: High-Altitude Illnesses (AMS, HAPE, HACE, Chronic Mountain Sickness)
clues: Also called chronic mountain sickness, it affects long-term high-altitude residents
Blunted hypoxic ventilatory drive triggers excessive polycythemia, blood hyperviscosity, and cor pulmonale
Descent to sea level provides definitive cure
Often called 'rapture of the deep,' it appears during air dives deeper than ~30 meters (4 ATA)
High lipid solubility of dissolved N2 in neuronal membranes mimics alcohol intoxication
Substituting helium ('heliox') for nitrogen prevents this hazard in deep commercial diving
Also known as 'the bends' or Caisson disease, it follows rapid ascent from a deep dive
Supersaturated nitrogen comes out of solution as bubbles in joints, blood vessels, and spinal cord white matter
Definitive therapy requires urgent recompression in a hyperbaric oxygen chamber
Pre-dive hyperventilation precipitates it by lowering PaCO2 and delaying the urge to breathe
During underwater ascent, falling ambient pressure causes PaO2 to plummet before PaCO2 reaches breakpoint
It causes sudden hypoxic loss of consciousness near the surface during breath-hold diving
It occurs at approximately 19 kilometers (62,000 feet) altitude where barometric pressure equals 47 mmHg
At this threshold, atmospheric pressure matches the vapor pressure of water at 37 C
Unprotected exposure causes exposed body fluids to vaporize spontaneously in a process called ebullism
In untrained adults it occurs around 50-65% of VO2max, shifting higher with endurance training
Bicarbonate buffering of rising lactic acid generates excess non-metabolic CO2
Above this exercise intensity, minute ventilation rises disproportionately relative to oxygen uptake
